extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; literary critics; attendees of lectures on poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the merits of English poets (Milton, Pope, Dryden, Shakespeare) focusing on versification, character, passion, imagination, style (natural vs artificial), and technical correctness. Draws on lecture examples and close readings to illustrate each criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of versification / modulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's verse 'floats up and down' with exquisite modulation; 'Milton has himself given us the theory of his versification — "Such as the meeting soul may pierce / In notes with many a winding bout / Of linked sweetness long drawn out."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versification should achieve a linked sweetness and natural modulation; other blank verse (Thomson, Young, Cowper, Wordsworth) is described as 'mere lumbering prose' when lacking Milton's insight into the 'hidden soul of harmony.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry of character and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential interest of a poem arises from the poetry of character and passion — e.g., the daring ambition and fierce passions of Satan and the paradisaical happiness and its loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how deeply characters' passions and ambitions are rendered; whether they furnish the poem's primary interest (rather than only fable or technical features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of heroic or suitable subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Satan is 'the most heroic subject that ever was chosen for a poem'; the suitability and loftiness of subject matter is a merit in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the subject admits grand treatment and whether the poet's selection amplifies the poem's scope and dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between magnitude of conception and strength of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The execution must be as perfect as the design is lofty; 'the strength is equal to the magnitude of the conception.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great conception must be met with comparable power of imagination, language, and structure; judge whether treatment matches ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness and distinctness of character depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever Satan is introduced he is 'gigantic, irregular, portentous, uneasy, and disturbed — but dazzling in its faded splendour, the clouded ruins of a god.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the concreteness of images and their consistency in making a character visually and psychologically present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate and striking imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of Satan are 'illustrated with the most striking and appropriate images' so that we 'see it always before us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images should fit character and occasion, illuminating rather than merely decorating; look for images that render abstractions tangible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological realism over cheap caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton avoids 'horns and tail' — bodily deformity used as a bye-trick — relying instead on depravity of will; he 'did not scruple to give the devil his due.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer moral/psychological complexity to simple physical caricature when depicting villainy; avoid relying on cheap emblems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical force and manly tone in speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches in Pandemonium show a 'decided manly tone' and 'eloquent dogmatism' as if each person spoke from thorough conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arguments, tone, and conviction in dramatic speeches — do they ring true to character and occasion and contribute to authority?

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation to impassioned prose as a poetic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's 'approximation to the severity of impassioned prose'—sometimes criticized—'is one of its great excellences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic diction may legitimately verge on impassioned prose when it heightens seriousness and gravity; judge such roughness as potential strength, not only a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blending pathos and sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages (e.g., angels' employments) are 'the most perfect example of mingled pathos and sublimity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the poem achieves both emotional tenderness and grandeur together, making abstract or noble scenes practically moving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating interest through repose and enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: Adam and Eve's portion of Paradise Lost contains 'little action... but there is much repose, and more enjoyment' — their bliss provides interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that lack of external action can still yield deep interest via atmosphere, innocence, and contemplative delight; judge success on quality of repose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate emotional tone (resignation vs intemperate passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pathos in Adam and Eve is 'mild contemplative' arising from regret and resignation, not 'fierceness of intemperate passion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match emotional intensity to subject and character; excessive passion where quiet resignation is fitting can destroy a scene's beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / representative power of imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet of nature 'holds communion with the very soul of nature' and 'sees things in their eternal beauty' so that works 'will last as long as nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a poet's imagination reaches universal human feelings and forms that continue to resonate across times and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and capacity to gratify different faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers judge merit not only by absolute worth but by 'originality and capacity of gratifying a different faculty of the mind, or a different class of readers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider originality and the particular intellectual or emotional faculty the poem addresses; a work may excel by serving a distinct aesthetic taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural style vs artificial style
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between poets of the natural (Chaucer, Spenser, Shakespeare, Milton) and the artificial (Dryden, Pope); the natural style is generally superior but leaders of the artificial deserve high rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poet's style arises organically from inner feeling and universal sympathy (natural) or from artifice, polish, and refined taste (artificial), and judge accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence in wit, refinement, and polished expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope's chief excellences: 'exquisite faculties, ... the most refined taste,' representing things as they appear to the indifferent observer, with concision and felicity of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value wit, elegance, concise phrasing, and refined perception when appropriate; these are strengths even if not 'lofty' in the romantic sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale of subject and diction (mock-heroic balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In The Rape of the Lock the balance between concealed irony and assumed gravity is 'as nicely trimmed as the balance of power in Europe' — the little is made great and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how successfully a poem sustains an ironic or mock-heroic tone: the equilibrium between high diction and trivial subject must be carefully controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and felicity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope's 'conciseness and felicity of the expression are equally remarkable' (example couplet: '*Tis with our judgments, as our watches ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the economy of language and the aptness of phrasing; epigrammatic clarity and compactness are marks of craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical rules should avoid narrow schoolishness
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'critical rules' in Essay on Criticism are 'too much those of a school, and of a confined one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of treating a confined set of rules as universal; effective criticism recognizes broader principles beyond a single school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical correctness and grammatical construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope 'is full of little errors. His grammatical construction is often lame and imperfect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention to grammar and construction matters; even great writers may have lapses that are worth noting when assessing polish and correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste, propriety, and social observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope shows 'quick tact for propriety of thought and manners as established by the forms and customs of society' and a 'refined sympathy with the sentiments ... of his family and friends.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a poet's sensitivity to social manners and propriety — how well the work reflects and manipulates social conventions and tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ornamentation vs substantive force
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope 'prefers the artificial to the natural in external objects' and often adorns trivial matters with splendour; 'the little becomes gigantic, the deformed beautiful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between ornament that enhances substance and ornament that substitutes for it; assess whether refinement masks lack of deeper force.
